name: Pedal to the Metal
subject: Cars and motoring
tagline: Twenty questions on badges, engines, races and the road. Starts easy, ends hard.

questions.q: Which Italian carmaker's badge is a prancing black horse on a yellow shield?
questions.w: Ferrari. The horse was the emblem of a First World War flying ace, Francesco Baracca, whose mother urged Enzo Ferrari to use it for luck.
questions.more: The yellow is the colour of Enzo's home town, Modena. Lamborghini's bull is the founder's star sign; Ferruccio Lamborghini made tractors until, legend says, Enzo Ferrari insulted him over a faulty clutch and he decided to build his own sports car.

questions.q: Which American brand has built the Corvette sports car since 1953?
questions.w: Chevrolet. The Corvette is the longest-running sports car still in production.
questions.more: The first ones were white, had six-cylinder engines and an automatic gearbox, and were so slow that sales nearly killed the model. Zora Arkus-Duntov, a Belgian-born engineer, turned it into a real performance car and is called the father of the Corvette. The brand's bow-tie badge was supposedly copied from hotel wallpaper in Paris.

questions.q: Which German brand's badge is four interlocking rings?
questions.w: Audi. The rings stand for the four companies that merged in 1932 to form Auto Union.
questions.more: Audi is Latin for 'listen', a translation of the founder August Horch's surname, which he could no longer use after leaving his first company. BMW's blue-and-white roundel is the flag of Bavaria, not a spinning propeller, whatever the adverts said in the 1920s.

questions.q: Toyota, Honda and Nissan are carmakers from which country?
questions.w: Japan, which overtook the United States as the world's biggest car producer in 1980.
questions.more: Toyota began as a loom-maker, and the family name is Toyoda; the spelling was changed because it takes eight brush strokes in Japanese, a lucky number. Toyota is the world's largest carmaker by volume. South Korea's Hyundai and Kia are now the third-largest group.

questions.w: Sport utility vehicle, a term that spread in the 1980s with the Jeep Cherokee and Ford Explorer.
questions.more: SUVs went from a niche to roughly half of all new cars sold worldwide by the 2020s, and the International Energy Agency has called them the second-biggest cause of rising carbon emissions in that period, after power generation. Their height is also why pedestrian deaths rose in the United States.

questions.q: Which Swedish carmaker invented the three-point seat belt in 1959 and gave away the patent so every manufacturer could use it?
questions.w: Volvo, whose engineer Nils Bohlin, a former aircraft ejector-seat designer, came up with it.
questions.more: The belt is estimated to have saved more than a million lives. Volvo means 'I roll' in Latin; the company began as a maker of ball bearings. It is now owned by China's Geely, which bought it from Ford in 2010.

questions.q: Which 24-hour endurance race has been held on public roads near a French town almost every June since 1923?
questions.w: The 24 Hours of Le Mans, where cars cover roughly 5,000 kilometres in a day and a night.
questions.more: The 1955 race saw the worst crash in motorsport history, when a Mercedes flew into the crowd and killed 83 spectators; Mercedes withdrew from racing for 30 years. Ford's four straight wins over Ferrari from 1966 to 1969 became the film Ford v Ferrari. Steve McQueen's 1971 film Le Mans nearly bankrupted him.

questions.q: At which race, nicknamed 'the greatest spectacle in racing', does the winner traditionally drink a bottle of milk in victory lane?
questions.w: The Indianapolis 500, run every Memorial Day weekend since 1911 on a two-and-a-half-mile oval.
questions.more: The milk tradition began with Louis Meyer, who asked for buttermilk after winning in 1936 because his mother said it was refreshing; a dairy executive saw the photo and made it permanent. Emerson Fittipaldi drank orange juice in 1993 to plug his own orchards and was booed for years. The track is big enough to hold the Vatican, Wimbledon and the Rose Bowl inside it.

questions.q: Who patented the first practical petrol-powered automobile in 1886?
questions.w: Karl Benz, whose three-wheeled Patent-Motorwagen is counted as the first car.
questions.more: His wife Bertha, who had financed the company with her dowry, took the car without telling him in 1888 and drove 106 kilometres to her mother's house, the first long-distance road trip, buying fuel at a chemist's and fixing a blocked pipe with her hatpin. Benz and Daimler worked a hundred kilometres apart and never met; their firms merged in 1926.

questions.q: The Tata Nano, launched in 2008 as the cheapest car in the world at about 2,000 dollars, was built in which country?
questions.w: India. Ratan Tata wanted a safe alternative to whole families riding on one scooter.
questions.more: It had one windscreen wiper, no radio and a two-cylinder engine behind the back seat. Sales never took off, partly because buyers did not want a car marketed as the cheapest, and production ended in 2018. Tata Motors also owns Jaguar Land Rover, bought from Ford that same year.

questions.q: A famous business-school legend claims a General Motors car sold badly in Latin America because its name means 'it doesn't go' in Spanish. Which car?
questions.w: The Chevrolet Nova. The story is false: it sold perfectly well in Mexico and Venezuela, and Spanish speakers no more hear 'no va' in 'nova' than English speakers hear 'not able' in 'notable'.
questions.more: The Pinto, on the other hand, really was a problem in Brazil, where the word is slang for small male genitals, and Ford renamed it Corcel. The Mitsubishi Pajero became the Montero in Spanish-speaking markets for a similar reason.
